entries.clue: Micropalaeontologist’s hiding a gemstone (4)

indicatorNotes.hiding: the long word conceals the answer inside itself

blocks.note: the gem sits in letters five to eight, straight after MICR

annotation.surface: A scientist who studies tiny fossils has a precious stone tucked away.
annotation.walkthrough: The absurdly long word is there to be looked inside: a gemstone buried in a scientist who digs through rock is a neat fit.
annotation.definitionFit: Opal is a gemstone prized for its shifting colours.

entries.clue: Duck, swans and egret – cold, not good – and everyone knows it! (4,6)

annotation.definitionNote: a clause standing for the noun phrase: an open secret is something everyone knows

indicatorNotes.not: 'cold, not good' puts C where G stood

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so O
a pen is a female swan
EGRET with C (cold) in place of G (good)

annotation.surface: A list of waterbirds on a chilly day, and apparently nobody is surprised.
annotation.walkthrough: Three birds in a row make it look like a birdwatching note; only the first two stay birds. A duck in cricket is a score of nought, hence O.
annotation.definitionFit: An open secret is something supposedly private that everyone actually knows.

entries.clue: Teetotallers ordering teas in bars (10)

indicatorNotes.ordering: the letters are put into a new order

annotation.surface: Non-drinkers asking for tea at the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link placing the teas inside the bars, but it is fodder too: all ten letters of 'teas in bars' are rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: Abstainers are people who refrain from drinking alcohol, just as teetotallers do.

entries.clue: Stemwinder repaired in Central America? (10)

annotation.definitionNote: an adjectival phrase for the adjective: the Midwest is the central region of the United States
annotation.surface: A wind-up watch gets fixed somewhere between Mexico and Panama.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Central America' normally means the isthmus south of Mexico; the question mark lets it mean the middle of the USA instead. A stemwinder is a watch wound by its stem, and also a rousing speech.
annotation.definitionFit: Midwestern describes the central states of America, such as Iowa or Kansas.

entries.clue: Everyman competes – with, in final stages, prize winner – in BBC shows (7)

annotation.definitionNote: read as a thing that shows the BBC: iPlayer is the service that streams its programmes

indicatorNotes.final stages: the last stage of each word is its final letter

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself, so I
last letters of prizE and winneR

annotation.surface: The setter enters a television contest and nearly takes the prize.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter's pseudonym in the clue usually means I or ME. iPlayer is the BBC's online streaming service; 'shows' is a verb here, not the programmes.
annotation.definitionFit: The BBC iPlayer is the app that shows BBC programmes online.

entries.clue: What implement niftily gyrates, nearing ultimate tightness primarily? (4,3)

annotation.definition: What implement niftily gyrates, nearing ultimate tightness primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: take each word's primary, or first, letter

blocks.clueFragment: What implement niftily gyrates, nearing ultimate tightness
blocks.note: first letters of What Implement Niftily Gyrates Nearing Ultimate Tightness

annotation.surface: A riddle about a small fixing spun round by hand until it is fully tight.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: the initials spell the answer, and the sentence describes it.
annotation.definitionFit: A wing nut has two flat wings so it can be spun by hand until tight.

entries.clue: Dealt a bad hand, left this mortal coil? (8,3)

blocks.note: cards are shuffled before dealing, and OFF means bad, as with milk
Hamlet's phrase for dying; the clue supplies the tail of the quotation

annotation.surface: A card player's luck runs out, fatally.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is playful rather than a dictionary sense: a shuffled deck gone off. The second borrows Hamlet's line, where shuffling off this mortal coil is dying.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are fair: cards mixed then gone bad, and Hamlet's idiom for dying, whose last words the clue quotes.

entries.clue: In uprising, be malevolent (4)

indicatorNotes.In uprising: in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom up

blocks.note: to be = to live, to exist

annotation.surface: A rebel movement turning nasty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like a revolt; in a down entry it is simply the instruction to write LIVE upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Evil and malevolent both mean wishing harm on others.

entries.clue: Badgers and horses (4)

blocks.note: to badger someone is to nag them
a nag is an old horse

annotation.surface: Two kinds of animal side by side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badgers' looks like the animal; it is the verb, pestering.
annotation.definitionFit: Badgers as a verb means pesters, which nags also means.

entries.clue: Few assets periodically offering direction (4)

indicatorNotes.periodically: at regular intervals, so every other letter

annotation.surface: A company with little capital is given some guidance now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Direction' reads as guidance for a struggling firm; here it is a compass point.
annotation.definitionFit: East is one of the four compass directions.

entries.clue: British genius’s drunk natural gin (4,6)

indicatorNotes.drunk: a drunk's letters stagger into a new order

annotation.surface: A brilliant Briton's tipple of choice turns out to be plain gin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' sits between genius and gin as if it describes him or the gin being consumed; it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Alan Turing was the British mathematician who helped break Enigma and founded computer science.

entries.clue: Friend of Oliver King has nickel-iron tool (7,5)

blocks.note: Stan (Stanley) Laurel, partner of Oliver Hardy

annotation.surface: A monarch called Oliver's pal owns a metal implement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oliver King' reads as one name; split it and Oliver points to Laurel and Hardy. A Stanley knife is the British name for a utility knife with a retractable blade.
annotation.definitionFit: A Stanley knife is a craft tool with a replaceable razor blade.

entries.clue: Relaxes, taking in clubs perhaps in informal attire (6,5)

indicatorNotes.taking in: one word takes the other inside it

blocks.note: clubs is one suit in a pack of cards; 'perhaps' flags the example

annotation.surface: Someone unwinds at a club in casual clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: LOUNGE(SUIT)S. 'Clubs' suggests golf clubs or nightclubs; it is the card suit. On a British dress code, 'informal' means a lounge suit, a business suit rather than black tie.
annotation.definitionFit: A lounge suit is the ordinary business suit that invitations call informal dress, one step below black tie.

entries.clue: Praise remark describing snarled lip (10)

indicatorNotes.describing: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one word goes round the other
indicatorNotes.snarled: snarled means tangled, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A kind word about someone's sneering mouth.
annotation.walkthrough: COM(PLI)MENT. 'Snarled' conjures a curled lip, but here it means tangled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a flattering remark is a piece of praise.

entries.clue: Son enrolled uncertainly having invested £1,000, and explored underwater (10)

indicatorNotes.uncertainly: the letters of ENROLLED are placed without certain order
indicatorNotes.having invested: the anagram takes K into itself, as money is put into a venture

blocks.note: K = a thousand, as in a £20k salary

annotation.surface: A boy hesitantly signs up for a course after paying a grand, then goes diving.
annotation.walkthrough: The financial word 'invested' is doing container work: the thousand goes inside the shuffled letters, not into a bank.
annotation.definitionFit: To snorkel is to swim face down breathing through a tube, exploring beneath the surface.

entries.clue: What William came to do with horse chestnut, you say? (7)

indicatorNotes.you say: flags a word spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: a conker is the seed of the horse chestnut, used in a British children's game

annotation.surface: William the Conqueror arrives in 1066, oddly equipped with a tree seed.
annotation.walkthrough: William is the Norman king who invaded England in 1066. Conkers is a British playground game of smashing horse chestnuts strung on laces.
annotation.definitionFit: The Norman duke's own title names his purpose in crossing the Channel in 1066: to take England by force.

entries.clue: Hamper with feathers from Siam, we’re told (3,4)

indicatorNotes.we’re told: flags words heard rather than read

blocks.note: Siam is the old name for Thailand, and down is soft feathers

annotation.surface: A basket stuffed with plumage imported from the Far East.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' looks like a picnic basket; it is the verb, to hinder.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: commitments that restrict someone's freedom are said to bind them in place.

entries.clue: Pieces of doom-laden rag edited in a fury (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a prepositional phrase for the adjective; both describe someone furious

indicatorNotes.Pieces of: the answer is made from parts of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'laden', through 'rag', into the start of 'edited'

annotation.surface: A gloomy newspaper gets edited by someone in a temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rag' is slang for a tabloid newspaper, which makes 'Pieces' look like articles; they are fragments of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone made furious by provocation is in a rage.

entries.clue: What a very young footballer might do, repeatedly? (7)

annotation.definition: What a very young footballer might do, repeatedly?

blocks.clueFragment: What a very young footballer might do
blocks.note: the surface reading: a skill a player shows, running with the ball at their feet
the setter's meaning: a baby, who lets saliva run from its mouth
the footballer's skill is a run of repeated small touches, and the baby does it over and over

annotation.surface: A question about a toddler kicking a ball about.
annotation.walkthrough: DRIBBLE is both the footballer's close control and a baby's drool; 'very young' is what brings in the second sense.
annotation.definitionFit: To dribble is both to run with the ball in small touches and, for a baby, to drool.

entries.clue: Monster in a fairy tale? (7)

blocks.note: an invented story, i.e. a big lie

annotation.surface: Asking whether an ogre features in a children's story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fairy tale' here is a made-up story, a lie, and 'Monster' is an adjective-like noun for something huge, not a creature.
annotation.definitionFit: A whopper is both something enormous and a blatant lie.

entries.clue: BMX trick from Jonathan Ross: honestly! (7)

indicatorNotes.Jonathan Ross: the presenter is known for pronouncing R as W, so the next word is heard in his voice

blocks.note: honestly! = really!, which Jonathan Ross says as 'weally'

annotation.surface: A TV host exclaims in disbelief at a stunt on a bike.
annotation.walkthrough: Jonathan Ross is a British chat-show host whose R sounds like W, so his 'really' becomes a wheelie.
annotation.definitionFit: A wheelie is riding a bike on its back wheel with the front lifted, a basic BMX trick.

entries.clue: Office ‘allies’ differing in everyday scene (1,5,2,4)

indicatorNotes.differing: the letters come out different from how they started

annotation.surface: Workplace friends falling out over something mundane.
annotation.walkthrough: The scare quotes around 'allies' suggest office friends who secretly disagree; the disagreement is the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A slice of life is a realistic depiction of ordinary, everyday experience.

entries.clue: Upset, curses celebrity (4)

indicatorNotes.Upset: in a down clue, set upward means read from the bottom

annotation.surface: An angry famous person swearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as angry; in a down entry it means turned up.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a famous performer is called a star, as in film star or TV star.

entries.clue: Poles’ uniform, grand and tight-fitting (4)

blocks.note: U in the NATO phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A Polish uniform that is splendid and close-fitting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like Polish people; it is the two ends of the earth.
annotation.definitionFit: Snug means fitting closely and comfortably.

entries.clue: Bouncer or 10 at Northern Ireland’s dance (6,4)

blocks.note: NI is Northern Ireland, plus the S of the possessive
a ball is a formal dance

annotation.surface: A nightclub doorman or someone at a Belfast dance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bouncer' wants to be a doorman; it is something that bounces. '10' looks like a cross-reference to 10 across but is just a number.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: 'bouncer' read literally as a thing that bounces, which a ball on court does constantly.

entries.clue: That man’s going to somewhere very hot (4)

annotation.surface: A man is heading off to a scorching destination.
annotation.walkthrough: HE'LL, 'he will', loses its apostrophe; the surface's hot holiday is the traditional fiery hell.
annotation.definitionFit: Hell is traditionally a place of fire, somewhere very hot.

entries.clue: Checked in to hotel and did sink in (10)

annotation.surface: A guest arrives at a hotel and flops onto the soft bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Did sink in' reads as sinking into a mattress; it means a fact was finally taken in.
annotation.definitionFit: To register is both to sign in at a hotel and to be understood or noticed.

entries.clue: Bolt, horse (4)

blocks.note: a bolt as a short metal fastener, not a dash

annotation.surface: A horse runs off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bolt, horse' reads as a command to a runaway animal; bolt is a fastener here.
annotation.definitionFit: A stud is a metal stud or fastener, and also a breeding stallion.
